title: Private deploy image revocation & canary rollback playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose
This is a working playbook for handling image revocation scenarios and orchestrating canary rollbacks in private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. It ties together: cosign-based image signing, attestation revocation signals, GitOps-driven ArgoCD rollbacks, Helm hooks for graceful cutover, and Terraform modules that enforce policy and admission webhooks.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to private-deploy clusters managed via ArgoCD (gitops) and Terraform-managed platform (tfstate in customer VPC or Redwood-managed state with remote backend).
- Images are signed with cosign and attestations are published to an internal attestation registry (Sigstore/OCI + optional TUF mirror).
- There is an image policy webhook (OPA/Gatekeeper or image-policy-webhook) enforcing signature/attestation checks at pull time.
- This playbook covers: detection -> validation -> automated soft-fallback -> manual rollback -> forensic & remediation.

Quick summary flow (TL;DR)
1) Detection: security/severity signal from attestation pipeline OR runtime image verification failure.
2) Immediate soft mitigation: scale down canary sync and pause ArgoCD sync for affected apps.
3) Fast rollback: ArgoCD automated rollback to last-known-good commit for canaries, coordinated with helm pre-upgrade hooks if needed.
4) Hard revocation: mark image as revoked in attestation registry, rotate KMS signatures if compromised.
5) Post-mortem: collect traces, image provenance, and update TF module to prevent recurrence.

Operators runbook (step-by-step)
- Step 0: Triage the alert
  - Who: on-call SRE / Private deployments rotation.
  - Where: alert in #onprem-ops Slack channel + PagerDuty if severity P1.
  - Minimum info to capture: image digest, repository, affected clusters/namespaces, ArgoCD application name, recent deploy git commit.

- Step 1: Quarantine the image (soft path)
  - If image attestation failed at deploy time: immediate action is to pause ArgoCD sync for the Application(s) and set a short-term deny in image-policy-webhook to prevent new pods from pulling the digest.
  - Commands (examples):
    - Pause ArgoCD: kubectl -n argocd patch application <app> -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' --type=merge
    - Add temporary deny rule (OPA): kubectl apply -f deny-temp-image-rule.yaml
  - Rationale: stop blast radius while preserving running replicas.

- Step 2: Rollback canary (automated soft rollback)
  - If the canary is using ArgoCD automated promotions, trigger a rollback to last successful Git tag/commit:
    - argocd app rollback <app> <previous-revision>
  - If Helm chart upgrade hooks are used to migrate state, run helm rollback with hook-allow-fail: helm rollback <release> <revision> --wait --timeout 5m
  - For multi-tenant installs, start with the canary namespace only, validate, then proceed to global rollback if signal persists.

- Step 3: Revoke at source (if confirmed malicious or broken)
  - Mark image digest as revoked in our attestation registry. Process depends on attestation backend:
    - Sigstore: publish revocation attestation pointing to digest with reason and operator id.
    - Internal registry: add a revocation flag and update OCI index.
  - Update image-policy-webhook data source to include revoked list (pull from signed revocation bundle).
  - If KMS or signing key suspected: rotate cosign key, publish new public key bundle to the admission controller config.

- Step 4: Post-rollback verifications
  - Smoke checks (automated): run smoke test suite for the app in canary namespace (script path: ops/smoke/canary-run.sh). Expect basic health endpoints and simple inference latency check < 250ms.
  - Observability checks: confirm error rates drop, CPU stays within expected band, no new image pull errors.

- Step 5: Communications and follow-up
  - Open a postmortem ticket (create in JIRA-OPS with template). Include traces, image provenance (git commit, builder, CI job id), and the timeline of actions.
  - Notify affected customers per SLA via support-runbook channel.

Terraform module notes (patterns & gotchas)
- Goal: keep image-policy-webhook, attestation-sink, and argocd config as reusable modules that customers can adopt/extend.
- Minimal module interface example (pseudo-TF in a string):
  module "image_policy" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//image-policy?ref=main"
    namespace = var.namespace
    cosign_public_keys = var.cosign_public_keys
    revocation_bucket = var.revocation_bucket
    webhook_service_account = module.k8s_sa.sa_name
  }
- Key design notes:
  - Keep revocation list remote (S3/GCS in customer VPC) to avoid needing cluster access to update the deny list. Webhook fetches periodically with signed bundle.
  - Use signed manifests for webhook config so attackers cannot inject deny lists. Bundle signed with cosign key and verified by webhook at startup.
  - Provide a "dry-run" flag for webhook to allow policy changes while testing.
  - Terraform state considerations: store minimal secrets in TF state; prefer referencing secrets in KMS or Vault rather than storing cosign private key in TF.

Helm and ArgoCD integration patterns
- Helm charts should include:
  - pre-upgrade and pre-delete hooks that can run smoke/backup tasks, e.g. snapshot DB before rolling back.
  - a helm value for "imagePolicySafePoint" which is a git commit or tag that ArgoCD can use as last-known-good.
- ArgoCD applications should be set with: syncPolicy: automated (prune: true, selfHeal: false) for canaries, but global apps default to manual sync for safety.
- Recommended ArgoCD workflow for canary:
  - Deploy to canary app (automated), run integration smoke via ArgoCD sync hooks, then promote to stable app by merging PR that updates stable app manifest reference.
  - Avoid automatic promotion across multiple clusters without explicit manual approval.

Image attestation and revocation model (practical)
- We support three layers:
  1) Build provenance: builder job id, CI pipeline link, git commit, SBOM.
  2) Signature: cosign signature proving private key ownership.
  3) Attestation: predicate documents (vulnerability scan, QA smoke results) attached via rekor/sigstore or internal attestation store.
- Revocation approaches:
  - Soft revoke: serve deny via webhook list (fast), but keep image in registry. Useful for immediate mitigation.
  - Hard revoke: delete image tag and add to registry denylist + publish attestation indicating revocation. Requires coordination with customers if image is reused.
  - Key rotation: if cosign private key compromised, rotate keypair and update webhook trust roots.

Automation & Playbooks we should build (todo)
- Auto-pauser: small operator that listens to attestation-sink and auto-pause ArgoCD apps matching affected image digests.
- Revocation bundle signer: pipeline that builds signed revocation bundles in S3 and triggers webhook config reload.
- Canary smoke runner: ArgoCD sync hook job template that runs smoke suite and reports back via slack + status to GitHub/PR.
- TF registry examples: publish stable module versions and example overlay that customers can copy.

Runbook quick checklist (short)
- [ ] Capture image digest + app + commit
- [ ] Pause ArgoCD sync for affected app(s)
- [ ] Apply temporary deny in webhook (or flip dry-run->enforce)
- [ ] argocd app rollback <app> <rev> or helm rollback
- [ ] Run smoke suite in canary namespace
- [ ] If confirmed malicious, publish revocation attestation + rotate keys
- [ ] Open postmortem and notify customers as needed

Troubleshooting notes (common failures)
- ArgoCD rollback stuck: check for resource hooks blocking (helm hooks waiting). Use kubectl get jobs -n <ns> and kubectl logs job/<job> to debug.
- Pods failing due to webhook timeout: increase webhook timeout in kubelet config or tune admission webhooks.
- Revocation bundle not picked up: verify S3/GCS IAM permissions and signature verification logs in the webhook.

Open questions / decisions needed
- Should we support hard-delete of images for customer-managed registries? legal/customer ops implications.
- What is our SLA for automated revocation plumbing (target: <5m from attestation signal to paused ArgoCD)?
- How should we surface revocation events to customers (email vs in-console alert vs webhook)?

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Cosign verify: cosign verify --key <pubkey> <registry>/<image>@sha256:<digest>
- Publish revocation attestation (pseudo): cosign attest --key $KEY --predicate revocation.json <image>@sha256:<digest>
- ArgoCD pause: kubectl -n argocd patch application <app> -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' --type=merge
- Trigger helm rollback: helm rollback <release> <revision> --wait

Notes to self: do a dry-run playbook test next week with staging attestation sink and simulated compromise. Capture metrics for time-to-pause and rollback success rate.

End of draft.
